title: Prediction of semiconductor interface electrical properties from processing history

concept.text: Discovered Materials grand challenge 02: predict how industrially relevant semiconductor interfaces form and acquire their electrical properties from growth, cooling and annealing. Sources given: https://discoveredmaterials.com/grand-challenges/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to MAS on 2026-11-15.
change_log.reason: Grand challenge published by Discovered Materials (Matforge Inc.), open as of November 2026 with a USD 1 million prize pool; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: Interfacial electrical properties from processing history
page.definition: A computational model maps semiconductor growth, cooling and annealing histories to interface structure and electrical properties. It predicts layer thicknesses, composition profiles, interface-trap density (electronic trapping states per area and energy) and fixed oxide charge.

goal.need: The 2005 ITRS reports a 2002 survey assessed by more than 70 integration/device engineers and managers at about ten Japanese semiconductor companies. Its estimates for selected successful applications of technology computer-aided design, meaning semiconductor process and device simulation, quantify reductions in development time, wafer lots and process options. The same roadmap identifies prediction of interface defects as a modelling requirement.

figures.caption: Reported reductions from semiconductor simulation in the 2002 survey
figures.note: Averages across the most successful cases surveyed; these are estimates for semiconductor simulation generally.

statements.body: The ITRS Modeling and Simulation working group requires models that predict interface defects.
statements.quote: Models that at least roughly predict effects like oxygen vacancies and Hf-Si interface states are required

statements.body: Discovered Materials includes semiconductor interface prediction among its funded Grand Challenges.
statements.quote: We commit $1 million in prize money to solutions to these challenges.
statements.context: The commitment covers five challenges, including this interface problem.

statements.body: NIST identifies interface prediction as a means of reducing device development time.
statements.quote: The ability to accurately predict interface behavior is critical for accelerating device development times
statements.context: The project page was updated on 2 October 2026.

completion.title: Matforge accepts a model as solving the Si/oxide interface Grand Challenge.
completion.criterion: Matforge determines that a reproducible process-history model meets every Challenge 02 criterion: agreement with measured layer thicknesses, composition profiles, energy-resolved interface-trap density and fixed oxide charge across all five interface classes, using one framework unchanged in form with declared parameters. Numerical acceptance tolerances are not published.
completion.set_by: Matforge, Inc., trading as Discovered Materials; Official Rules, Sections 4–5, incorporating the Challenge 02 description.
completion.threshold_quote: Sponsor is the sole judge of whether a submission meets a challenge's success criteria.
completion.basis: The rules incorporate the technical description and reserve the determination of success to Matforge. This supplies an external acceptance test while leaving numerical accuracy to the sponsor's judgement. Challenge 02 was listed as open on 14 November 2026.

milestones.title: A model reproduces a semiconductor interface’s measured layer thicknesses.
milestones.criterion: Match measured oxide thickness for an interface class. Published partial results include planar Si growth at 700–1300 °C, 0.1–1.0 atm and 30–2000 nm thickness (1965); stress-retarded nonplanar Si oxidation (1988); and face-dependent 4H-SiC oxidation at 950–1150 °C in 1 atm dry O₂ (2004). Other designated benchmarks measure oxygen transport in 2–5 nm Hf-based films (2011) and Ge oxide (2017), and model SiGe thickness/composition (2005). These address formation and transport, without establishing electrical prediction across the five classes.
milestones.set_by: Discovered Materials, Challenge 02, thickness component of Predictive accuracy; applicable separately to each interface class.

milestones.title: A model predicts the direction of processing-induced changes in interface-trap density.
milestones.criterion: Predict the observed direction of an electrical response to processing; hydrogen annealing reducing interface-trap density is the challenge's example. The 1990 planar-Si benchmark studied four orientations at 750–1100 °C, with and without hydrogen-containing post-metal anneals. Both interface-trap charge and fixed oxide charge increased as oxidation temperature decreased. This measured trend is a reproduction target, rather than evidence that a predictive model passed it.
milestones.set_by: Discovered Materials, Challenge 02, qualitative assessment before quantitative assessment; its hydrogen-anneal example does not prescribe an anneal for every class.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether a hydrogen anneal reduces D_{it}

milestones.title: A model quantitatively reproduces an interface’s measured structure and electrical properties.
milestones.criterion: Quantitatively match an interface class’s measured thicknesses, composition profiles and electrical data from its processing history. The initial electrical benchmark uses planar (100), (110), (111) and (511) Si. This test applies separately to each case; completion additionally requires one unchanged framework across all five. No numerical error tolerance is specified.
milestones.set_by: Discovered Materials, Challenge 02, quantitative Predictive accuracy assessment; its initial electrical benchmark is specifically planar Si/SiO₂.
milestones.threshold_quote: Agreement with the measured thicknesses, composition profiles and electrical data.

not_found: No numerical error tolerances, runtime limit or specified blinded holdout protocol were found in the challenge description or official rules.
No separate standard defining completion of process-history prediction of interface electrical properties was found in searches of ITRS/IRDS, NIST and ASTM material.
A complete electrical validation dataset and demonstrated predictive result for every interface class could not be established from the designated benchmark sources.
Several publisher pages were inaccessible; institutional records and author-posted copies supplied the corresponding paper text or abstracts.

results.finding: Planar Si/SiO₂: model reproduced measured growth kinetics from four sources over oxide thicknesses of 1–100 nm.
results.detail: Experimental curves were scaled to overlap the theoretical curve. Pressure scaling was imperfect at long growth times, and the model departed from thick-film kinetics.
results.quote:
These predictions were tested with kinetic curves taken
from references [6,27–29], corresponding to oxidations in
Joule-eﬀect heated and rapid thermal processing furnaces
in a variety of growth parameters (temperature, O 2 pres-
sure, and time) leading to oxide thicknesses ranging from
1 to 100 nm.

results.finding: Si nanowire oxidation model matches measured oxide thickness; sample size not stated; initial radius 25 nm.
results.detail: The comparison used previously reported measurements at 1223 K. The text reports good agreement but does not quantify the thickness error.

results.finding: A model predicted Si/SiO₂ interface-trap annealing kinetics across 2 crystal orientations; device sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The model reproduced the observed decrease in interface-trap density during annealing over 170–500 °C. Aluminum-gate MOS capacitors were studied.
results.quote:
This model sucessfully predicts anneal kinetics over a temperature range of 
170--500 cC, representing a 106 dynamic range in anneal rates.

results.finding: DFT model of one Ge/GeO₂ interface configuration: two substituted Y atoms passivated its gap states.
results.detail: The calculation supports a passivation mechanism consistent with the reported reduction in interface-trap density. It does not calculate the change in interface-trap density or establish that the modeled configuration reproduces the observed electrical response.
results.quote:
A useful 
example is shown in Fig 5(a,b) which shows two substitutional Y’s separated from the Ge side, 
which were separated by a previous O vacancy. This configuration is fully passivated, with no gap 
states even in the GeO2.
